blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 11 (Special Theory of Relativity), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question of 5 marks (define, explain, derive) is followed by a numerical of 3 marks on the same topic. Each question has a model answer; the numericals are solved step by step.

blocks.prompt: 1 Explain that all motion is relative. Describe the experiment of a ball dropped inside a train compartment (i) when the train is at rest and (ii) when it moves with uniform velocity vₒ, and state what it shows. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Motion is relative: Direction depends on the observer; a ball thrown to your right appears to go to the left of a person facing you. Rest and motion also depend on the observer: the walls of a moving train seem stationary to its passengers but moving to a person on the ground. We cannot say whether an object is absolutely at rest or in motion; all motions are relative to the observer or to the reference frame being used.

Experiment: An observer in a closed train compartment uses the compartment as his frame of reference. He drops a ball and measures the horizontal distance it travels, the vertical fall taking the same time t in each case.

Case (a), train at rest: The horizontal velocity of the ball is zero, so its horizontal distance is zero. The ball falls to a point on the floor directly below the point of release (Fig. 11.1-a). Observers inside and outside the train see the same thing.

Case (b), train moving with uniform velocity vₒ: On release the ball has an initial horizontal velocity vₒ and behaves like a projectile. In time t it travels a horizontal distance vₒt. The train and the observer inside also move vₒt in the same time, so the observer inside sees the ball fall to the point directly below where it was dropped. An observer outside sees the ball follow a projectile path (Fig. 11.1-b).

Conclusion: Observers in different frames of reference, moving with uniform velocity relative to each other, perceive the same motion differently.

book_ref.quote: An observer in a closed train compartment uses the compartment as his frame of reference.

blocks.prompt: 2 A train moves with a uniform velocity of 20 m s⁻¹. A passenger drops a ball which takes 0.6 s to reach the floor. Find the horizontal distance moved by the ball (i) for an observer on the ground and (ii) relative to the point below the release point, for the passenger. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: The ball keeps the train's horizontal velocity; the train and passenger move the same distance in the same time.

book_ref.quote: It travels a horizontal distance vₒt in time t it takes for the ball to reach the floor.

steps: Ground observer: horizontal distance = vₒt = 20 × 0.6 = 12 m
Train and passenger also move vₒt = 12 m in the same 0.6 s
Relative to the passenger, distance = 12 m − 12 m = 0 m: the ball lands directly below the release point
blocks.final_answer: (i) 12 m along a projectile path; (ii) 0 m, the ball lands directly below

blocks.prompt: 3 State the two postulates of the special theory of relativity. Using them, explain time dilation: define proper time, write the equation for the dilated time and show that a moving clock runs slow. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Postulates:
1. The laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames (Principle of Relativity). There is therefore no way to detect absolute uniform motion.
2. The speed of light in free space has the same value for all observers, regardless of the state of motion of the source or the observer (Principle of Constancy of Light); c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Since c is constant, space and time become relative.

Time is not absolute: According to the special theory, time depends on the motion of the frame of reference.

Proper time: An observer stationary in an inertial frame measures the time interval between two events in that frame. This interval tₒ is the proper time.

Dilated time: If the observer moves relative to the frame of the events with relativistic velocity v (or the frame moves relative to the observer), he measures not tₒ but
t = tₒ/√(1 − v²/c²) ... (11.1)

Moving clocks run slow: √(1 − v²/c²) is always less than one, so t is greater than tₒ; time has dilated (stretched) due to relative motion. This applies to all timing processes, physical, chemical and biological; even aging slows at relativistic speeds. Example: an event taking 1 s for a traveler on a plane moving at 0.8 c takes about 1.7 s for a person outside.

book_ref.quote: Suppose an observer is stationary in an inertial frame and measures the time interval between two events in this frame.

blocks.prompt: 4 An unstable particle lives for 2.0 μs when at rest. It moves through a laboratory at 0.96 c. Find (i) its lifetime as measured in the laboratory and (ii) the distance it travels in the laboratory before it decays. (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: The rest lifetime is the proper time; the laboratory measures the dilated time, and distance = speed × time.

blocks.prompt: 5 What is length contraction? Define proper length, write the relation for the contracted length, state the direction in which contraction occurs, and illustrate it with an example. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Length contraction: The distance from the Earth to a star measured by an observer in a moving spaceship appears smaller than the distance measured by an observer on the Earth. If you move relative to two points a fixed distance apart, the distance between them appears shorter than if you were at rest relative to them. This effect is length contraction.

Proper length: The length of an object, or the distance between two points, measured by an observer at rest relative to them is the proper length ℓₒ.

Relation: If the object and observer are in relative motion with speed v, the contracted length is
ℓ = ℓₒ√(1 − v²/c²) ... (11.2)
Since √(1 − v²/c²) is less than one, ℓ is less than ℓₒ.

Direction: Length contraction occurs only along the direction of motion; no contraction is observed perpendicular to it.

Example: A train 100 m long at rest travels at 0.8 c. A person inside measures 100 m. A person beside the track finds
ℓ = 100 × √(1 − 0.64) = 100 × 0.6 = 60 m.

book_ref.quote: The distance from Earth to a star measured by an observer in a moving spaceship

blocks.prompt: 6 A spaceship is 80 m long at rest. Find (i) its length measured by an observer at rest when it flies past at 0.6 c and (ii) the speed at which this observer would measure its length as 40 m. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: 80 m is the proper length; use ℓ = ℓₒ√(1 − v²/c²) forwards for (i) and backwards for (ii).

blocks.prompt: 7 Explain how the mass of an object varies with its speed according to the special theory of relativity. Use the relation to show what happens as v approaches c, and explain why Newton's laws still work in everyday life. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Mass is variable: The mass of an object depends on its speed. The mass measured at rest is the rest mass mₒ; when moving at speed v the object has an increased mass m:
m = mₒ/√(1 − v²/c²) ... (11.3)
Since √(1 − v²/c²) is less than one, m is greater than mₒ.

Meaning: The increase in mass indicates an increase in inertia at high speeds. As v approaches c, a greater force is needed to change the object's speed.

Limit v → c:
As v → c, v/c → 1, therefore √(1 − v²/c²) → 0
Thus m → ∞
An infinite mass would need an infinite force to accelerate it. Infinite forces are not available, so an object cannot be accelerated to the speed of light c in free space.

Everyday life: Everyday speeds are extremely small compared with c. Even Earth's orbital speed is only 30 km s⁻¹ while c is 300,000 km s⁻¹, so m ≈ mₒ and Newton's laws are valid. For subatomic particles moving close to c, relativistic effects are very prominent and Einstein's equations are needed.

book_ref.quote: According to the special theory of relativity, the mass of an object is a variable quantity

blocks.prompt: 8 A body has a rest mass of 5.0 kg. Find (i) its mass when it moves at 0.6 c and (ii) the speed at which its mass would be 2.5 times its rest mass. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use m = mₒ/√(1 − v²/c²) directly for (i); for (ii) set m/mₒ = 2.5 and solve for v.

book_ref.quote: will have an increased mass m when observed to be moving at speed v

blocks.prompt: 9 Starting from Einstein's relation E = mc², obtain the expressions for (i) rest mass energy, (ii) relativistic kinetic energy and (iii) the change in mass Δm for a change in energy ΔE. What does the last result tell us about nuclear reactions? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Mass and energy are distinct entities but are interconvertible. The total energy E and mass m of an object are related by
E = mc² ... (11.4)
where m depends on the speed of the object.

(i) Rest mass energy: At rest m = mₒ, so the energy equivalent of the rest mass is
Eₒ = mₒc²

(ii) Kinetic energy: A moving object has m greater than mₒ, so mc² is greater than mₒc². The difference (mc² − mₒc²) is due to the motion and is its kinetic energy:
K.E. = mc² − mₒc² = (m − mₒ)c²

(iii) Change in mass: From Eq. 11.4, a change in energy ΔE changes the mass by
Δm = ΔE/c²

Meaning: c² is a very large quantity, so small changes in mass correspond to very large changes in energy. Everyday energy changes are too small to give measurable mass changes, but the energy and mass changes in nuclear reactions are found to be exactly in accordance with these equations.

book_ref.quote: mass and energy are distinct entities but are interconvertible

blocks.prompt: 10 A body of rest mass 0.20 kg moves at 0.6 c. Find its (i) rest mass energy, (ii) total energy and (iii) kinetic energy. (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find the moving mass first; then Eₒ = mₒc², E = mc² and K.E. = (m − mₒ)c².

book_ref.quote: As mc² is greater than mₒc²

blocks.prompt: 11 Explain the relativity of simultaneity with the example of a train fitted with light-operated doors. Then use the hypothetical spaceship journey to a star to show how observers on the Earth and in the spaceship explain the shorter journey time. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Relativity of simultaneity: Two events at different places that are simultaneous for one observer are generally not simultaneous for another observer in a frame moving relative to the first. Whether two events are simultaneous depends on the observer's frame of reference.

Train with light-operated doors: The light switch is at the centre of the roof and is operated by a traveler standing in the middle of the compartment. The train travels at half the speed of light and the traveler turns on the light. The light travels forward and backward at equal speed and reaches both doors at the same time, so the traveler sees both doors open simultaneously. An observer outside sees the back door open before the front door, because the back door moves towards the light waves while the front door moves away from them.

Hypothetical spaceship journey: A spaceship travels to a star at half the speed of light and takes 8 years from the point of view of an observer on the Earth.
Earth's view: the clocks on the spaceship run slowly (time dilation), so less time passes on the spaceship than on the Earth.
Occupants' view: the length of the journey has contracted (length contraction), so they cover it in less time.
Both views agree: the occupants record about 7 years instead of 8 (8 × √(1 − 0.25) = 6.9 years).

book_ref.quote: For the spaceship occupants, the length of the journey has contracted

blocks.prompt: 12 A spaceship travels to a star at 0.6 c. Observers on the Earth find that the journey takes 15 years. Find (i) the time recorded by the occupants and (ii) how much less they age than people on the Earth during the journey. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Earth time is the dilated time of the ship's clocks; the occupants' time is smaller by the factor √(1 − v²/c²).

book_ref.quote: Let a spaceship be travelling to a star with half of the speed of light.
